Extraction: Autonomous Agentic AI Architectures for Optimizing Security Operations Centers (SOC) KPIs: Methodology, Impact on Detection, Response, and Recovery

Miroslav Stefanov; Kristyan Stefanov; Laxima Niure Kandel; Sean Crouse (Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, Daytona Beach, USA); Boyan Jekov (University of Library Science and Information Technology, Sofia, Bulgaria)
2025; Land Forces Academy Review, Vol. XXX, No. 3(119), pp. 479-493; DOI 10.2478/raft-2025-0046. Venue is NOT INDEXED in Scopus/SJR (mandatory stratum caveat, PDR-0007).

SOCs face alert fatigue from the large volume of false-positive alerts that burdens analysts and raises the risk of overlooking genuine threats, delayed responses due to lack of prioritization and fragmented incident management, and insufficient accuracy in event classification that distorts KPI metrics and reduces report reliability (Abstract, p. 479; §1, p. 480). Since KPIs such as TTD, TTR, MTTR, and SIER are the fundamental instrument for assessing SOC detection, response, and recovery maturity (§1, p. 480), the study targets an integrated intelligent system for automated KPI management that adaptively reduces alerts, accelerates response, and improves metric-assessment accuracy (§1, p. 480).

An Agentic AI architecture of ten specialized agents covering the full SOC security/operations lifecycle (§3.3, pp. 483-484): TTD Monitoring Agent (rule-based, no ML; computes timestamp_occurred vs timestamp_detected and alerts on threshold breaches, p. 483); FNR Analysis Agent (XGBoost classifier, recommends mitigation playbooks, p. 483); FPR Suppression Agent (XGBoost plus dynamic suppression; auto-filters alerts with severity < 3 and logs actions in detection_rules.json, p. 483); TTR Response Agent (LightGBM regressor; on detected delays automatically triggers predefined playbook scenarios and notifies teams, pp. 483-484); IRR Tracking Agent (task-closure ratio with automated reminders, p. 483); SIHR Validation Agent (remediation-checklist completeness alerts, pp. 483-484); MTTR Recovery Agent (LightGBM regressor; simulates automated task assignment when thresholds are exceeded, p. 484); OE Task Agent (on-time task proportion with reminders below 30%, p. 484); CSR Feedback Agent (fine-tuned BERT classifying feedback as Positive/Neutral/Negative in real time, p. 484); SIER Metrics Agent (rule-based incidents-to-events ratio with threshold alerts, p. 484). Agents operate as an integrated system with consistent information exchange and shared model/config files (clf_fpr.model, clf_fnr.model, reg_ttr.txt, reg_mttr.txt, detection_rules.json) (§3.3, p. 484). The agentic paradigm is non-LLM: rules plus classical ML (XGBoost, LightGBM, fine-tuned BERT), with no LLM reasoning or orchestration layer.

Design-and-demonstration study on real and publicly available data: 214 CSV files (5,270.09 MB; 25,182,806 initial records) cleaned to 8,628,160 observations with 343 unique columns (§3.1, p. 481), consolidated into a unified schema from CICIDS2017, CSE-CIC-IDS2018, CTU-13 Botnet Dataset, Elastic Security Example Datasets, and Wazuh Cloud Demo, emulating SIEM event/alert logs, Incident Management, Task Tracking, and CRM/feedback logs (§3.1, pp. 481-482). Five ML models on three algorithms (Table 1, p. 482; §3.2, pp. 482-483): two XGBoost classifiers (FNR, FPR), two LightGBM regressors (TTR, MTTR) trained offline with periodic monthly retraining (§3.2, p. 483), and a fine-tuned BERT sentiment analyzer for CSR trained 20 epochs on an 80%/20% train/test split (§4.3, pp. 486-487). Evaluation combines internal model metrics (Accuracy/F1/AUC, Table 2, p. 484; MAE/MSE/R², Table 3, p. 486; loss curves, Figure 3, p. 487) with one end-to-end demonstrative execution of the agent workflows on the prepared dataset, reported via console logs and visualizations of computed KPI values and triggered actions (§4.4, pp. 487-491). No comparative baseline, no ablation, and no deployment in a live SOC.

Not specified quantitatively — the paper executes no empirical comparison against a concrete baseline (no before/after measurement and no non-agentic control), so no MTTD/MTTR reduction can be attributed. The abstract's claim of "reduced detection and response times" (Abstract, p. 479) is supported only by (a) internal model-quality metrics — TTR regressor MAE 18%, MSE 1000, R² 0.85; MTTR regressor MAE 20%, MSE 1160, R² 0.80 (Table 3, p. 486) — and (b) KPI readouts from a single demonstrative run: TTD measured at 0.01 seconds against a 3-minute threshold (§4.4.1, p. 488); all 11 processed incidents showed TTR between 655 and 4192 minutes, exceeding the 300-minute threshold and auto-generating warnings (§4.4.2, p. 489); the MTTR model predicted 1884.2 hours, triggering automated task assignment (§4.4.3, p. 490); IRR 85.6% vs 90% threshold and 49 incomplete remediation checklists also triggered alerts (§4.4.2, p. 489). These are outputs of the system itself (internal model values and threshold checks), not measured improvements relative to any baseline SOC process.

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Contributes a task-specialized agent-per-KPI design pattern in which each of the ten agents couples one metric to monitoring, prediction, and automated action — playbook triggering, alert suppression, task auto-assignment, reminders, and notifications — with coordinated information exchange across agents (§3.3, pp. 483-484). Demonstrates feasibility of agentic KPI automation over 8.6M+ rows "without the need for manual intervention in most processing phases" (Abstract, p. 479). Reported model performance: FNR classifier Accuracy 80%, F1 0.76, AUC 0.78 outperforms the FPR classifier (Accuracy 65%, F1 0.71, AUC 0.74) (Table 2, p. 484), with jagged ROC curves attributed to smaller or imbalanced test sets (§4.1, p. 485); the BERT model kept Eval Loss stable at ~1.02-1.06 with no overfitting signs (§4.3, pp. 486-487). Claimed advantages are modularity, flexibility, scalability, and reduced team workload and alert-fatigue risk (§5, p. 491). The paper exemplifies the rules-plus-classical-ML (non-LLM) strand of agentic SOC automation, a useful contrast class for LLM-based multi-agent frameworks.

Authors acknowledge that building the architecture requires substantial initial resources, a high level of expertise, and continuous model maintenance through periodic retraining, and that excessive automation risks insufficient attention to new or unexpected threats falling outside the scope of pre-trained agents (§5, pp. 491-492). Future work: integrating continual learning for adaptation to emerging threats, applying Explainable AI (XAI) to increase transparency and trust in automated decisions, and additional research in real operational environments for more robust validation (§5, p. 492). Implicit limitations evident from the text: single demonstrative execution with no baseline or control (§4.4, pp. 487-491), public/benchmark datasets rather than a live SOC (§3.1, pp. 481-482), and only moderate FPR-classifier performance (Accuracy 65%, Table 2, p. 484).

Relevant as architectural evidence for an agent-per-KPI design that directly instruments the thesis's target metric family — detection (TTD/FPR/FNR) and response/recovery (TTR/MTTR) — with autonomous playbook triggering and task auto-assignment (§3.3, pp. 483-484) that resemble copilot actuation in incident response, plus a reusable catalog of 16 indicators in 4 KPI categories (§2, pp. 480-481). However, it provides no causal evidence that an agentic system reduces MTTD/MTTR, since no baseline comparison is executed (§4.4, pp. 487-491). The study enters the corpus with the mandatory stratum caveat — Land Forces Academy Review is NOT INDEXED (NÃO INDEXADO, PDR-0007) — and represents a non-LLM agentic paradigm (rule-based agents plus XGBoost/LightGBM/BERT), contrasting with the LLM-centric copilots central to the thesis; it is best used as a comparison point on the agentic-autonomy spectrum and as KPI-instrumentation groundwork.

Medium — directly proposes a ten-agent Agentic AI architecture for SOC KPI automation explicitly targeting TTD/TTR/MTTR with automated playbook triggering, but the evidence is a demonstrative execution with internal model metrics only (no empirical baseline comparison), the paradigm is non-LLM (rules + classical ML), and the venue is not indexed (PDR-0007).
